column2: Gilgameš rose to unravel a dream,
saying to his mother:
The mother of Gilgameš, who knows everything,
said to Gilgameš:
He lay down, and he saw a second;
he rose and spoke to his mother:

Mother, I have seen a second:
27-28	[ ... ] in the street [of Uru]k-of-the-Squares
29-30	an axe was lying, and around it they gathered,
31	an axe — and strange was the look of it.
32	I saw it, and I rejoiced;
33-34	I loved it like a wife, murmuring over it;
35-36	I took it up and set it at my side.
The mother of Gilgameš, clever, expert, all-knowing, [said] t[o Gilgameš:]
— because I shall make him your equal.
While Gilgameš unravels the d[re]am,
Enki[du sat] before the harlot;
the two of them fell to lo[vi]ng one another.
He forgot the open la[n]d where he was born.
For seven days and seven nights
En[kidu,] aroused, poured himself into Ša[mha]t.
The har[lot] shaped her [m]outh
and said to Enkidu:

I look at you, Enkidu: you are become like a god.
54-55	Why go roving the open land with the beasts?
56-57	Come — let me lead you into [Uru]k-of-the-Squares,
58	to the holy house, the seat of Anu.
59	Enkidu, rise; let me take you
60	to [Eann]a, the s[e]at of Anu,
61	where the rites are [est]ablished —
62-63	and you t[oo, li]ke a man, will fi[nd yourself] a place there.
64-65	Enough! You are set(?) on ground that is a shepherd's beat.
He heard her w[o]rd; her speech found favor:
the coun[s]el of the woman st[r]uck home in his heart.
She stripped [off] a single garment and clothed him in it;
in a second garm[e]nt she dressed herself.
Holding his hand, like a god she leads him
to the shepherds' cam[p], the pl[a]ce of the sheep-pen.
The shepherds gathered around him:

Lik[e ... ]
80	[Why, he is the image of Gilgameš in outline —]
81-82	[shorter in stature, but big in the bone!]
83-84	[Likely it is he who was born in the hills:]
85-86	the milk of the wild beasts is what he sucked.
They set bread before him:
he squints, and he stares, and he peers —
Enkidu does not know bread for eating;
beer for drinking he has never learned.
The harlot shaped her mouth and said to Enkidu:

Eat the bread, Enkidu — the mark of life;
98	drink the beer — the custom of the land!
Enkidu ate the bread until he was full;
of the beer he drank seven goblets.
His mood ran free; he was singing;
his heart grew light, and his face began to shine.
The barber worked over his shaggy body;
he anointed himself with oil and turned into a man;
he put on a garment: there he is — like a bridegroom!
He took his weapon; he went hunting lions;
the sh[ephe]rds could lie down at night:
he battered the wo[l]ves; he chased off the lions;
the senior herdsmen slept —
Enkidu was their watchman, a wakeful man.
A certain young man was hu[rr]ying to the [weddin]g(?)-house,
With [Ša]mkat he is making merry;
then he raised his eyes: he caught sight of the man.
He said to the harlot:

Šamkat — fetch the man away.
141-142	Why has he come? His errand I would hear.
The harlot hailed the man;
she came up to him; he talked with her:

Young man — where are you hurrying?
146	What is your toilsome march for?
The young man shaped his mouth
and said to E[nkidu:]

They have invited me into the wedding-house:
150-151	it is the lot of the people to contract the marriage-tie.
152	I shall heap the ceremonial table
153	with the merry fare of the wedding-house —
154	for the king of Uruk-of-the-Squares
155	the people's veil(?) stands open for the taking of the bride;
156	for Gilgameš, king of Uruk-of-the-Squares,
157-158	the people's veil(?) stands open for the taking of the bride:
159	he couples with the destined wife —
160-161	he first, and the husband after.
162	By the counsel of the god it is decreed:
163-164	from the cutting of his birth-cord she was appointed his.
At the young man's word his face went pale.
[ ... ] let me se[e] your [in]tent [ ... ]
He goes i[n front,] and Šamka[t] behind him.
He entered inside Uruk-of-the-Squares,
and the crowd gathered about him;
he stood there in the street of Uruk-of-the-Squares,
and the people, gathered, were talking over him:

Why, he is the image of Gilgameš in outline —
184-185	[sh]orter in stature, but [b]ig in the bone!
186-187	Li[kely it is he who] was born in [the h]ills:
188-189	the milk of the wild bea[st]s is what he sucked.
In Uruk the regular offerings were laid on;
the young men made holiday; a champion was set up
for the young man whose looks were fair —
for Gilgameš, as for a god, a counterpart was set up.
For Išhara the bed was laid,
and Gilgameš was to jo[i]n with the girl that night.
Then he came striding up — he took his sta[nd] in the street
and block[ed the p]ath of Gilgameš.
[The young men(?) massed] around him.
He loo[ms(?) ... ]
Gilgameš [ ... the do]or(?) [ ... ]
against hi[m ... ]
he loom[s(?) ... ]
E[nkidu] rose against him, face to face,
and they met in the Great Square of the land.
Enkidu with his foot barred the door;
he would not let Gilgameš enter.
They grappled — bent low like champion bulls,
they wrecked the doorpost; the wall shuddered;
Gilgameš and Enkidu grappled, and bent low like champion bulls,
they wrecked the doorpost; the wall shuddered.
Then Gilgameš knelt, one foot to the ground;
his fury quieted; he turned his chest away.
When he had turned his chest away,
Enkidu said to him, to Gilgameš:

As one all your own your mother bore you —
236-237	the Wild Cow of the Sheepfold, Ninsun!
238	High is your head over fighting men:
239-240	the kingship of the people Enlil decreed for you.
Second tablet.
Surpassing all kings — (the series continues.)
